learningObjectives: Apply design thinking stages to a real-world design problem.
Convert user research findings into a clearly defined problem statement.
Create focused how-might-we questions for ideation.

activities.title: Design Thinking Map
activities.instruction: Explore how each design thinking stage contributes to solving a user problem.

content.concept: Design thinking uses empathy, definition, ideation, prototyping, and testing to solve user-centered problems iteratively.
content.tip: Select each stage to understand what designers do and what output it produces.

items.label: Empathize
items.description: Understand users, their context, behaviors, and needs.

items.label: Define
items.description: Synthesize research into a focused problem.

items.label: Test
items.description: Evaluate solutions and learn from user feedback.

activities.title: Problem Statement Builder
activities.instruction: Arrange the elements of a focused user problem statement.

content.concept: A strong problem statement identifies the target user, their need, and the meaningful problem without prescribing a solution.
content.tip: Do not include a proposed interface or feature in the problem statement.

activities.title: How Might We Lab
activities.instruction: Transform user problems into focused, open-ended design questions.

content.concept: How-might-we questions reframe user problems as open opportunities for generating multiple possible solutions.
content.tip: A strong HMW question should be open enough to encourage ideas but focused enough to remain connected to the problem.

scenarios.question: Users struggle to find relevant internship opportunities among hundreds of listings. Which HMW question is most useful?
options: How might we help users discover relevant internships more easily?
How might we build a blue filter button?
How might we force users to read every listing?
scenarios.correctAnswer: How might we help users discover relevant internships more easily?
scenarios.explanation: The question focuses on the user problem without prescribing a specific solution.

scenarios.question: Users abandon a long registration form because it feels overwhelming.
options: How might we make registration feel easier to complete?
How might we add five more fields?
How might we use a larger logo?
scenarios.correctAnswer: How might we make registration feel easier to complete?
scenarios.explanation: The question creates space for multiple possible solutions.

activities.title: Problem Validation
activities.instruction: Select the problem statement that is best supported by research evidence.

content.concept: A well-defined problem should connect directly to research evidence and a meaningful user need.
content.tip: Choose the statement that describes an observed user problem rather than a proposed feature.

pairs.prompt: Users interviewed repeatedly reported difficulty comparing internship opportunities.
pairs.answer: Users need an easier way to compare relevant opportunities.

pairs.prompt: Users said they frequently forget which applications they have already submitted.
pairs.answer: Users need clearer application status tracking.

pairs.prompt: A designer thinks users would like an AI chatbot.
pairs.answer: Not enough evidence to define a validated problem.

choices: Users need an easier way to compare relevant opportunities.
Users need clearer application status tracking.
Not enough evidence to define a validated problem.
